title: Malaysia | BNM Risk Management in Technology, Cybersecurity and Customer Information
tagline: Protect systems, customers and data the Malaysian way: RMiT, the NCII code, MCIPD breaches, scams and the amended PDPA.
sectors: Bank contact centres and branch networks
Bank technology, cybersecurity and operations teams
Bank risk, compliance, privacy and audit functions
Boards and senior management of Malaysian banks
description:
This quest teaches staff of Malaysian conventional banks the technology, cybersecurity and customer information rules set by **Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM)**: the **Risk Management in Technology (RMiT)** policy document (in force from 28 November 2025 and reissued on 25 September 2026 with a **code of practice for national critical information infrastructure (NCII) entities** under the **Cyber Security Act 2024**), the **Management of Customer Information and Permitted Disclosures (MCIPD)** policy document of 31 October 2025, BNM's business continuity notification rules, and the **Personal Data Protection Act 2010** as amended in 2024, including data protection officers and breach notification from 1 June 2025.

RMiT requires every bank to give **all staff** technology and cybersecurity awareness education **at least annually**, to train technology, cyber and risk staff continuously, and to keep the board trained. MCIPD requires staff awareness, training and reminders on protecting customer information and on breach escalation. This quest serves those duties for all staff, with deeper material for managers, incident teams and directors.

Five stages follow a fictional team at Bukit Kenanga Bank Berhad from governance to scams, breach notification, cloud and the PDPA, with real BNM cases.

This quest builds knowledge of the rules and good practice; it does not replace your bank's own policies, procedures or advice from your security, data protection and compliance teams.
audience: All staff of Malaysian conventional banks who use the bank's systems or handle customer information
Contact centre and branch staff who help customers facing phishing, scams and account takeover
Technology, cybersecurity and incident response teams who run controls and notify regulators
Risk, compliance, data protection and internal audit staff who oversee RMiT, MCIPD and PDPA duties
Senior managers and directors accountable for technology and cyber risk oversight
outcomes: Explain who is accountable under RMiT and the awareness and training duties in paragraphs 8.4(c) and 15.1 to 15.3
Apply everyday cyber and customer information controls: access, MFA, logs, devices and messaging tools
Recognise phishing, scams and account takeover, and apply RMiT's digital fraud and customer protection rules
Escalate and notify cyber incidents and customer information breaches to BNM, NACSA and the PDP Commissioner on time
Describe RMiT and outsourcing duties for third parties and cloud, and the amended PDPA's DPO and breach rules
Summarise the evidence a bank needs to show BNM that its technology and information programme works

quest.name: The Kenanga Firewall
quest.premise: You have just joined the Technology Risk and Cybersecurity Office of Bukit Kenanga Bank Berhad, a fictional conventional bank headquartered in Kuala Lumpur with an operations hub in Cyberjaya and branches from Penang to Kuching. The bank has just been told the reissued RMiT applies in full, and BNM's supervisors will review its programme next quarter. With CISO Farah Nadia, SOC lead Ravi, data protection officer Tan Mei Ling, contact centre leader Hafiz and board technology committee chair Datuk Andrew Ong, clear five stages, then face the final boss: the supervisors' exam.

sessions.title: RMiT Foundations: Board, Management, CISO and the Awareness Duty
sessions.summary: Meet BNM's RMiT policy document: why it exists, what 'S' and 'G' mean, the duties of the board, senior management and the CISO, and the training duties in paragraphs 8.4(c) and 15.1 to 15.3 that make this quest compulsory.
objectives: Explain the purpose, legal basis and structure of RMiT, including standards marked S and guidance marked G
Describe the board's technology oversight duties, including the designated committee and paragraph 8.4
Describe the roles of senior management, the cross-functional committee and the CISO
Apply the awareness and training duties in paragraphs 15.1, 15.2 and 15.3 to different groups of staff

cards.title: Stage one: the control tower
cards.setting: Level 30 meeting room, Bukit Kenanga Bank head office, Kuala Lumpur. Monday, 8:45 am.

lines.text: Your new pass says 'Technology Risk and Cybersecurity Office'. On the screen, a thick PDF is open: Risk Management in Technology, issued 25 September 2026.
Welcome! I'm Farah, the bank's CISO. That document is RMiT, BNM's rulebook for technology and cyber risk. It shapes almost everything we do.
Andrew Ong, I chair the board technology committee. BNM is clear: the board approves the technology risk appetite and must understand cyber risk. Directors don't get to say 'that's IT's problem'.
Ravi, security operations. My team watches the systems around the clock. But most attacks still start with a person clicking something.
Mei Ling, data protection officer. When customer information leaks, BNM's MCIPD rules and the PDPA land on my desk at the same time.
(video call from Cyberjaya) Hafiz, contact centre. My agents take scam calls from frightened customers every day. They need answers they can use.
And RMiT says every one of our staff needs cybersecurity awareness at least once a year. So your mission: five stages, from this tower to the phone queue. Ready?

scenes.heading: Who sets the rules
scenes.narration: Bank Negara Malaysia issues RMiT under the Financial Services Act 2013. It applies to licensed banks and other financial institutions, and the current version took effect on 28 November 2025.

scenes.heading: Why it exists
scenes.narration: Banks run on complex systems and face fast-changing digital crime. RMiT sets minimum standards so that banks prevent disruption, protect customers and stay resilient against cyber-attack.

scenes.heading: Proportionate, not optional
scenes.narration: Larger, more digital and more connected banks must adopt stronger controls. Size changes how much you do, not whether you comply.

scenes.heading: S and G
scenes.narration: Paragraphs marked S are standards that must be met, and breaking them can lead to enforcement. Paragraphs marked G are guidance that BNM encourages banks to adopt.

scenes.heading: September 2026
scenes.narration: The reissue added Appendix 12, a code of practice for banks designated as national critical information infrastructure under the Cyber Security Act 2024.

cards.title: Who owns technology risk under RMiT
cards.caption: RMiT spreads accountability from the board to every user. Enforcement under paragraph 1.3 can reach the institution and its directors, officers and employees.

items.label: Board
items.detail: Approves technology risk appetite, IT and cyber strategy, and the risk frameworks; oversees through a designated committee.

items.label: Senior management
items.detail: Primary responsibility for day-to-day technology and cyber risk; turns frameworks into policies.

items.label: CISO and risk function
items.detail: Independent of daily IT operations; advises, sets policy and enforces compliance.

items.label: Technology, SOC and CERT
items.detail: Run controls, monitoring, incident response and recovery.

items.label: Every staff member
items.detail: Follows policy, spots threats and reports quickly; trained at least annually.

cards.question: What does a paragraph marked 'S' in RMiT mean for a bank?
options: It is a standard that must be complied with, and a breach can lead to enforcement action
It is a suggestion that the bank may adopt if it has the budget
It applies only to banks designated as NCII entities
It is a sample practice that BNM will publish for comment
cards.explanation: RMiT defines S as a standard or requirement that must be met; non-compliance may result in enforcement. G marks guidance that is encouraged. NCII status is a separate question handled in Appendix 12.

cards.title: What the board must do
cards.body:
RMiT gives the board clear duties (paragraphs 8.1 to 8.5):

- **Risk appetite**: approve a technology risk appetite aligned with the bank's overall appetite, with tolerances, risk owners and key risk indicators.
- **Strategy and frameworks**: approve IT and cybersecurity strategic plans covering **at least three years**, and oversee the technology risk management framework (TRMF) and cyber resilience framework (CRF).
- **Policy reviews**: make sure IT policies are reviewed **at least once every three years** unless RMiT says otherwise.
- **Committee**: designate a board-level committee for technology matters with **at least one member with technology experience**.
- **Paragraph 8.4**: get regular updates on technology risk and cyber threats, give real time to discussing extreme cyber scenarios, and **take part in cybersecurity awareness and training** (8.4(c)).
- **Audit**: the board audit committee makes sure technology audit is effective and gaps are closed.

cards.title: Match the RMiT role
cards.prompt: Link each role to the duty RMiT gives it.

pairs.right: Approves the technology risk appetite and joins cybersecurity awareness and training
Supports the board's technology oversight; includes a member with technology experience
Bears primary responsibility for day-to-day technology and cyber risk
Guides technology plans; approves policy deviations and reports material ones to the board
Runs the technology risk function, independent of daily IT operations, and is appropriately certified
Ensures technology audit is effective and corrective actions close promptly

cards.title: Three training duties in RMiT section 15
cards.caption: Section 15 is why this quest exists. Each paragraph targets a different group.

items.left: All staff (and third parties where appropriate)
items.right: Technology and cyber awareness, at least annually, updated for new threats, effectiveness measured

items.left: Technology operations, cyber and risk staff
items.right: Adequate, continuous training so they are competent and suitably certified
Regular training and information on technology developments for oversight

items.label: 8.4(c)
items.right: Take part in relevant cybersecurity awareness and training programmes

lines.text: Last year's awareness module: 96% completion. HR is pleased. I'm not.
Same video as the year before. And our phishing test click rate didn't move at all.
Two directors skipped it. They said the board gets a cyber briefing anyway.
RMiT asks for more than a completion rate. It says the education must reflect the evolving threats and that we measure whether it works.
Then the board needs a decision. What do we change before BNM looks at it?

cards.title: Fixing the awareness programme
cards.situation: Bukit Kenanga's annual cyber awareness module has not changed in two years. Completion is high, simulated phishing results are flat, two directors did not take part, and the bank's outsourced contact centre staff are not included. Andrew asks you to propose the fix.

choices.text: Refresh the content for current threats, measure effectiveness with tests and phishing simulations, bring directors in, and add relevant third-party staff
choices.outcome: This meets paragraph 15.1 (annual, current, measured, third parties where appropriate) and paragraph 8.4(c) for the board. The board can now see evidence that behaviour is changing.

choices.text: Keep the module but make completion a performance target for all staff
choices.outcome: Completion improves, but the content is still stale and nobody measures whether behaviour changes. RMiT asks for both currency and measured effectiveness.

choices.text: Exempt directors, since they receive a quarterly cyber briefing in the board pack
choices.outcome: A briefing is useful, but RMiT separately requires the board to take part in cybersecurity awareness and training and to receive regular training on technology developments.

choices.text: Leave third-party staff out, because they are the vendor's responsibility
choices.outcome: RMiT expects the bank to include third-party service providers in relevant training where appropriate, and its service agreements should require them to take part.

cards.back: Technology risk management framework: how the bank defines, assesses, controls and monitors technology risk as part of enterprise risk management.
Cyber resilience framework: governance, objectives and tolerance for cyber risk, covering identify, protect, detect, respond and recover.
A system supporting critical banking services whose failure could significantly harm customers, operations, finances, reputation or compliance.
A cyber event that harms the security of a system or its data, whether malicious or not.
Chief information security officer: responsible for the technology risk function, independent of daily IT operations, with enough authority and resources.
A bank designated by BNM as national critical information infrastructure under the Cyber Security Act 2024; Appendix 12 applies to it.

cards.question: Under paragraph 15.2 of RMiT, which staff must receive adequate and continuous training so that they are competent and suitably certified?
options: Staff involved in technology operations, cybersecurity and risk management
All customer-facing staff in branches and contact centres
Only the CISO and the head of internal audit
Only staff of third-party cloud providers
cards.explanation: Paragraph 15.2 targets technology operations, cybersecurity and risk management staff. All staff are covered by the annual awareness duty in 15.1, and the board by 15.3 and 8.4(c).

cards.title: Real cases: BNM penalties for system downtime
cards.caption: RMiT paragraph 10.32 caps unplanned downtime of critical customer-facing systems at 4 hours a year (rolling) and 120 minutes per incident. Source: BNM enforcement notices.

items.label: Malayan Banking Berhad, July 2024
items.detail: Mobile banking platform downtime, June 2023 to May 2024; a matching penalty went to a group entity.

items.label: CIMB Bank Berhad, July 2024
items.detail: Disruptions on 8 and 9 April 2024 to e-banking, ATMs and cards.

items.label: Bank Simpanan Nasional, June 2025
items.detail: Repeated downtime, June 2023 to October 2024.

items.label: Downtime cap per incident
items.detail: Maximum tolerable downtime per incident for critical systems.

cards.title: Real case: what the downtime penalties teach the board
cards.body:
In August 2024 BNM published penalties on **Malayan Banking Berhad** and **CIMB Bank Berhad**, imposed on 29 July 2024, for breaching RMiT's high-availability thresholds for critical systems. In July 2025 it published a **RM995,000** penalty on **Bank Simpanan Nasional**.

BNM's notices pointed to root causes that sit with management and the board, not just engineers:

- Maybank could not recover **effectively and promptly**, and resilience improvements BNM required were **incomplete** when the incidents happened.
- CIMB and BSN had **lapses in executing response and recovery** to restore systems quickly.

BNM weighed the impact on customers, the failure to take reasonable steps, past compliance and the effectiveness of remediation. The lesson: the board's approved risk tolerances, strategy and investment plans are tested in real outages, and BNM checks whether recovery actually works.

cards.title: Stage one take-aways
items: RMiT is BNM's binding policy document on technology and cyber risk; 'S' paragraphs must be met, 'G' paragraphs are guidance.
The board approves technology risk appetite and three-year IT and cyber plans, oversees through a designated committee, and must join cyber awareness training (8.4(c)).
Senior management runs technology risk day to day; the CISO is independent of IT operations and appropriately certified.
Paragraph 15.1: all staff get technology and cyber awareness at least annually, kept current, with effectiveness measured and third parties included where appropriate.
Paragraph 15.2 covers continuous training for technology, cyber and risk staff; 15.3 covers regular board training on technology developments.

cards.prompt: Think about the last cybersecurity awareness training you took. Did it reflect threats you actually see in your job? What one change would make it more useful for your team?

quiz.question: From which date did the current version of BNM's RMiT policy document take effect, according to the reissued document?
options: 25 September 2026
1 June 2023
26 August 2024
28 November 2025
quiz.explanation: RMiT states it comes into effect on 28 November 2025 unless a paragraph says otherwise. 25 September 2026 is the reissue date that added Appendix 12; 26 August 2024 is when the Cyber Security Act 2024 came into effect.

quiz.question: A paragraph in RMiT is marked 'G'. How should the bank treat it?
options: As a standard whose breach automatically leads to a fine
As a rule that only applies to e-money issuers
As guidance that BNM encourages the bank to adopt
As a draft that has no effect until gazetted
quiz.explanation: G marks guidance, such as advice or recommendations that are encouraged. S marks standards that must be complied with, where non-compliance may lead to enforcement.

quiz.question: Against whom can BNM take enforcement or supervisory action for breaching an 'S' paragraph of RMiT?
options: Only the institution as a legal entity, never individual directors or staff
Only the CISO named in the bank's responsibility map
Only third-party providers that caused the breach
The institution and its directors, officers and employees
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 1.3 says action can be taken against the institution including its directors, officers and employees. Accountability is not limited to the entity or to one role.

quiz.question: What must the composition of the board-level committee designated for technology matters include?
options: A majority of members who have previously served as a bank CISO
The CISO as a voting member of the committee
A representative of BNM sitting as an observer
At least one member with technology experience
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 8.3 requires the designated committee to include at least one member with technology experience and competencies. The CISO advises the board but is not required to be a member.

quiz.question: Which item is part of paragraph 8.4 of RMiT on board discussion of technology and cyber risk?
options: The board must personally test the bank's incident response plan every month
The board must take part in relevant cybersecurity awareness and training programmes
The board must hold a cybersecurity certification before appointment
The board must approve every change to firewall rules
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 8.4 requires regular updates, enough time to discuss cyber risks, and participation in cybersecurity awareness and training (8.4(c)). The other options are not RMiT requirements.

quiz.question: The cross-functional technology committee approves a deviation from an IT security policy. Under RMiT, what else must happen if the deviation is material?
options: It must be reported to the board
It must be approved by BNM before it takes effect
It must be published on the bank's website
It must be reversed within 30 days
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 8.7(c) lets the committee approve deviations after a robust risk assessment, with material deviations reported to the board. RMiT does not require BNM approval or publication.

quiz.question: A bank appoints its head of IT infrastructure as CISO while he keeps running data centre operations. Which RMiT requirement does this most clearly put at risk?
options: The rule that the CISO must be based outside Malaysia at group level
The rule that the CISO reports only to internal audit
The CISO's independence from daily technology operations
The rule that the CISO must hold a law degree
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 9.4 requires the CISO to be independent from day-to-day technology operations, with sufficient authority, independence and resources. The other options are not RMiT rules.

quiz.question: Under paragraph 15.1, how often must cybersecurity awareness education be given to all staff?
options: Only at induction, with refreshers left to each department to decide
Once every three years, in line with policy reviews
At least annually, kept up to date with evolving threats
Only after a major cyber incident at the bank
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 15.1 requires cybersecurity awareness education at least annually, kept up to date with evolving threats, with its effectiveness measured. The three-year cycle applies to policy reviews, not awareness.

quiz.question: A bank's awareness programme reports only completion rates to the board. What does paragraph 15.1 also require?
options: Publishing completion rates for every department in the annual report
Measuring whether the programmes are effective
Sending completion data to BNM every quarter
Replacing classroom sessions with e-learning
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 15.1 requires the bank to measure the effectiveness of its education and awareness programmes, not just record attendance. RMiT does not require publication or quarterly submissions to BNM.

quiz.question: In BNM's 2024 and 2025 downtime cases against Malayan Banking Berhad, CIMB Bank Berhad and Bank Simpanan Nasional, which RMiT thresholds were breached?
options: No more than 8 hours of downtime a month and 4 hours per incident
No more than 24 hours of downtime a year and 6 hours per incident
No more than 4 hours of unplanned downtime a year and 120 minutes per incident
No more than 1 hour of downtime a quarter and 30 minutes per incident
quiz.explanation: The notices cite paragraph 10.32: cumulative unplanned downtime affecting customers of no more than four hours on a rolling 12-month basis, and a maximum of 120 minutes per incident.

sessions.title: Cyber Defence Every Day: Resilience Framework, Access, Monitoring and Customer Data Controls
sessions.summary: See how RMiT's cyber resilience framework, security operations centre, access controls, MFA and logging work in practice, and how MCIPD's ICT controls stop customer information leaving through screens, USB drives and messaging apps.
objectives: Describe the cyber resilience framework, the SOC, threat intelligence and red team testing under RMiT
Apply RMiT's access control principles: deny by default, least privilege, time-bound access, segregation and MFA
Apply MCIPD controls on portable devices, messaging platforms, screen photos and unusual access to customer data
Explain what BNM found in its 2026 cybersecurity and customer information case

cards.title: Stage two: the watch floor
cards.setting: Security operations centre, Bukit Kenanga operations hub, Cyberjaya. Tuesday, 2:10 am.

lines.text: Wall screens glow in the dark. One tile turns amber: 'Unusual download volume: customer statements, user ID LN4471'.
That's a loan officer in Penang. Four thousand statements downloaded at two in the morning. That isn't a normal shift.
(on the phone) Could be a stolen password. Could be an insider. Either way, RMiT and MCIPD both expect us to catch exactly this.
Account suspended. Session killed. The logs are preserved. Now we find out how it got this far.
Welcome to stage two. Tonight you'll see why access rules, monitoring and logs matter more than any firewall.

scenes.heading: A framework, not a product
scenes.narration: RMiT requires a cyber resilience framework that sets the bank's governance, objectives and tolerance for cyber risk, and aims for resilience against extreme but plausible attacks.

scenes.heading: Five functions
scenes.narration: The framework must support identifying, protecting, detecting, responding and recovering, for systems on the bank's premises and those run by third parties.

scenes.heading: Layers of defence
scenes.narration: Banks build layered defences using sound practices such as zero trust, defence in depth through micro-segmentation, and security by design.

scenes.heading: Always watching
scenes.narration: A security operations centre monitors all critical systems continuously, and threat intelligence looks outward, including social media and the dark web, for data leaks and false rumours about the bank.

scenes.heading: Think like an attacker
scenes.narration: At least once every three years, a red team simulates a realistic attack to find weaknesses before criminals do.

cards.title: Identify, protect, detect, respond, recover
cards.caption: RMiT paragraph 11.2 expects the cyber resilience framework to support all five functions, on premises and at third parties.

items.label: Identify
items.detail: Know critical systems, data, assets and connections; keep an automated asset inventory.

items.label: Protect
items.detail: Layered controls, zero trust, access control, encryption and secure configuration.

items.label: Detect
items.detail: SOC monitoring, threat intelligence and prompt investigation of anomalies.

items.label: Respond
items.detail: Incident response plan, CERT, crisis management and communication.

items.label: Recover
items.detail: Restore services fast, learn lessons and strengthen defences.

cards.question: How often must a bank run a realistic red team simulation attack on its infrastructure under RMiT?
options: At least once every three years
Every month
Only when BNM directs it
Once, before going live with a new system
cards.explanation: Paragraph 11.6 requires a realistic red team exercise at least once every three years. The annual cyber drill under paragraph 11.16 is a different test of the incident response plan.

cards.title: Access control: the RMiT principles
cards.body:
RMiT (paragraphs 10.53 to 10.57) sets the rules every system owner and user lives with:

- **Deny all by default**: no access unless explicitly authorised.
- **Least privilege**: only the minimum permissions needed for the role.
- **Time-bound access**: limited to the period the work needs.
- **Segregation of incompatible functions**: no one person can develop, run and secure a system alone.
- **Dual authorisation** for activities the bank defines as high risk.
- **Strong authentication**: stronger for remote access and critical activities; each credential tied to **one user**.
- **MFA for critical systems** that resists social engineering, combining two or more of something you know, are or have.
- **Access matrix** reviewed periodically.
- **Logs** of user activity in critical systems kept for **at least three years** and reviewed.

Sharing your login breaks the one-user-one-credential rule and destroys the audit trail.

cards.title: Within the rules or a breach?
cards.prompt: Sort each action at Bukit Kenanga by whether it fits RMiT and MCIPD controls or breaks them.

items.text: A contractor's admin access expires automatically when the project ends
Two tellers share one login to save time at a busy branch
A developer also approves and deploys her own code to production alone
Access to recorded customer calls is limited to staff who need it
A relationship manager photographs a customer's account screen to show a colleague
USB ports are disabled for staff with no need to store customer data
A staff member sends a customer's statement through a personal messaging app
Critical system activity logs are kept for three years and reviewed

cards.title: Two documents, one control environment
cards.caption: RMiT protects systems; MCIPD focuses on customer information. Banks apply both.

items.label: Prevent
items.left: Deny by default, least privilege, MFA for critical systems
items.right: Preventive and detective ICT controls against theft, loss and disclosure

items.label: Devices
items.left: Secure storage and transport of sensitive data on removable media
items.right: Only staff with a business need download to bank-issued devices, protected by encryption

items.label: Detect
items.left: SOC monitoring and prompt investigation of anomalies
items.right: Detect unusual frequent viewing, suspicious downloads and unauthorised disclosure

items.label: Evidence
items.left: Critical system logs kept at least three years
items.right: Audit trail reviews and random sample checks

cards.title: The desktop messaging app
cards.setting: Mortgage processing team, Kuala Lumpur head office. Tuesday, 10:20 am.

lines.text: I've just seen something on the proxy report. Someone in mortgages is logged into a desktop messaging app on a work PC.
Half my old team used to do that. Customers send their payslips that way. It's faster than email.
Faster for fraudsters too. MCIPD says we must restrict web-based messaging and social media for staff who handle customer information, especially end-to-end encrypted ones.
So what do we tell the customer who just sent a payslip on that app?

cards.title: Working from home with customer files
cards.situation: Aisyah, a credit analyst, has a deadline. She asks if she can copy 300 customer credit files to her personal USB drive to work at home tonight. Her team leader is on leave. You are the most senior person in the team today.

choices.text: Say no to the personal drive; help her use the bank's approved remote access on a bank laptop, or escalate for a bank-issued encrypted device if she has a business need
choices.outcome: Right call. MCIPD allows downloads only by staff with a legitimate need onto bank-provided, protected devices, and requires controls for offsite work such as strong remote authentication and encryption.

choices.text: Allow it if she encrypts the USB drive with a password
choices.outcome: Encryption helps, but a personal drive is outside the bank's control and MCIPD limits downloads to devices the bank provides. The bank cannot monitor or recover the data.

choices.text: Allow it, since she is a trusted employee and will delete the files tomorrow
choices.outcome: Trust is not a control. If the drive is lost, this becomes a customer information breach that the bank may need to notify to BNM and the PDP Commissioner.

choices.text: Tell her to email the files to her personal email instead, because email is encrypted
choices.outcome: Sending customer data to a personal account is an unauthorised disclosure risk and moves data outside the bank's controls entirely.

cards.title: The cyber-attack lifecycle
cards.prompt: RMiT paragraph 11.8 asks banks to set defences for each phase of an attack. Put the phases in order.
steps: Reconnaissance: the attacker studies the bank and its staff
Weaponisation: the attacker builds a malicious payload
Delivery: the payload arrives, often in an email or link
Exploitation: a weakness or a click lets the code run
Command and control: the attacker steers the compromised device
Exfiltration: data is taken out of the bank

cards.back: Every time you step away. An unlocked screen lets anyone act under your credentials, and your login is your accountability.

cards.front: MFA prompt you did not request
cards.back: Deny it and report it at once. It may mean someone has your password and is trying to log in.
Install only through the bank's approved process. Unapproved tools can carry malware and bypass controls.
Follow the bank's acceptable use policy; NCII entities must set a BYOD rule, enabling or restricting it.
Never. MCIPD requires banks to restrict messaging and social platforms for staff handling customer information.
Report it quickly through the bank's channel. Early reports shrink damage and help meet notification deadlines.

cards.question: Which detection mechanism does MCIPD specifically require for customer information?
options: Prompt detection of unusual frequent viewing and suspicious downloading of customer information by staff
A monthly survey asking staff whether they have shared customer data
Annual confirmation from each customer that their data is correct
A review of staff social media accounts by human resources
cards.explanation: Paragraph 10.23 requires mechanisms to promptly detect unauthorised access, unusual frequent viewing, suspicious downloads and unauthorised disclosure. Surveys and customer confirmations are not what the paragraph requires.

cards.title: Real case: Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad
cards.caption: Source: BNM press release of 1 April 2026 and its enforcement register.

items.label: External intrusion
items.detail: An external threat actor gained unauthorised access to the institution's IT infrastructure.

items.label: BNM findings
items.detail: Breaches of RMiT and MCIPD traced to inadequate cybersecurity controls and incident response.

items.label: Penalty imposed
items.detail: Administrative monetary penalty of RM1,000,000 under the Development Financial Institutions Act 2002.

items.label: Penalty paid
items.detail: The institution paid in full and strengthened controls, resources and governance.

items.label: Published
items.detail: BNM published the action and restated what RMiT and MCIPD require.

cards.title: Real case: what BNM said about the 2026 cyber breach
cards.body:
On **20 January 2026** BNM imposed an administrative monetary penalty of **RM1,000,000** on **Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad**, a development financial institution, after an **external threat actor gained unauthorised access** to its IT infrastructure.

BNM found breaches of both documents:

- **RMiT**: cybersecurity controls and **incident response** were inadequate.
- **MCIPD**: preventive and detective **ICT controls**, their regular monitoring, and mechanisms to spot unauthorised access, unusual viewing or downloads and unauthorised disclosure of customer information fell short (paragraphs 10.12, 10.13 and 10.23).

BNM weighed the severity, lack of reasonable care, existing controls, past record and how well the institution fixed the gaps.

**Your lesson**: the detection rules in this stage are not paperwork. When an intruder gets in, BNM asks whether your monitoring would have caught unusual access, and whether staff escalated in time.

cards.title: Stage two take-aways
items: The cyber resilience framework must support identify, protect, detect, respond and recover, on premises and at third parties.
Banks need a SOC covering all critical systems, cyber threat intelligence (including the dark web), and a red team exercise at least every three years.
Access is denied by default, least privilege and time-bound, with segregation of duties, one credential per user and MFA for critical systems.
Critical system activity logs are kept for at least three years; sharing logins destroys accountability.
MCIPD limits downloads to bank devices, restricts messaging and social platforms, and requires detection of unusual viewing and downloads.

cards.prompt: List the systems you log into each day. For each one, do you have only the access your role needs? Is there any access you no longer use that you should ask to remove?

quiz.question: Which five functions must the cyber resilience framework support under RMiT paragraph 11.2?
options: Identification, protection, detection, response and recovery
Planning, purchasing, patching, policing and publishing
Prevention, prosecution, penalty, publicity and payment
Inventory, insurance, investigation, isolation and invoicing
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.2 requires the CRF to support effective identification, protection, detection, response and recovery of systems and data, whether hosted on premises or by third parties.

quiz.question: Bukit Kenanga's threat intelligence team spots a forum post on the dark web offering what looks like the bank's customer data. Which RMiT duty is this team fulfilling?
options: Running the annual cyber drill that must be reported to the board
Performing the data centre resilience and risk assessment
Testing the out-of-band communication channel
Gathering threat intelligence, including on data leaks and false rumours
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.10 requires a threat intelligence process to detect cyber threats including data breaches and misleading information, drawing on sources such as social media and the dark web.

quiz.question: A new branch officer is given access to every module of the core banking system 'just in case'. Which RMiT principle does this break?
options: Least privilege
Dual authorisation for high-value payments
Time-bound access for external contractors
Segregation between network operations and network security
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.54(b) requires least privilege: only the minimum permissions needed for legitimate users to do their roles. Access 'just in case' is the opposite.

quiz.question: What does RMiT require of multi-factor authentication for user access to critical systems?
options: It must rely on SMS one-time passwords for every user who logs in to critical systems
It must resist social engineering and combine two or more factor types
It is optional where staff use strong passwords
It must use biometrics as one of the factors
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.55 requires MFA that can defend against social engineering, combining two or more of knowledge, inherent and possession factors. Biometrics are one option, not a requirement.

quiz.question: For how long must activity logs of users in critical systems be kept under RMiT?
options: At least seven years, without a review requirement
At least twelve months, reviewed annually
At least three years, with regular and timely review
Until the end of the user's employment
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.57(c) requires logs of user activity in critical systems to be kept for at least three years and reviewed regularly. Seven years appears in MCIPD for breach investigation reports, not system logs.

quiz.question: A systems engineer can change the core banking code, deploy it to production and switch off the security logging himself. Which RMiT principle is missing?
options: Default transfer limits for new customers
Customer notification of new controls
Segregation of incompatible functions
Annual review of the outsourcing plan
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.54(d) requires segregation so that no single person can independently modify, circumvent and disable security features, for example separating development from operations and security administration from system administration.

quiz.question: Under MCIPD, who may download customer information to portable storage devices?
options: Any staff member, provided they delete the data within one week of downloading it to any device
Only branch managers, onto their personal devices
Only staff with a business need, onto bank-provided devices protected by encryption
Any staff member who has completed induction training
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 10.16 and 10.17 restrict downloads to staff with a legitimate business need, onto bank-provided devices protected with controls such as passwords and encryption.

quiz.question: Why does MCIPD require banks to restrict access to web-based messaging and social media platforms for staff who handle customer information?
options: To improve staff productivity during working hours and reduce personal use of bank time
To stop customer information leaking to outsiders over the internet
To reduce the bank's internet bandwidth costs
To comply with advertising rules for financial products
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 10.22 targets the risk of customer information leaving the bank through web-based messaging and social media, particularly end-to-end encrypted platforms, where the bank cannot see what is sent.

quiz.question: MCIPD gives examples of ways to deter staff from disclosing customer information without authority. Which is one of them?
options: Paying staff a bonus for every month in which no customer complains about privacy
Letting staff keep customer files at home
Restricting personal devices in high-risk areas such as call centres
Allowing open use of personal phones on dealing floors
quiz.explanation: Guidance in paragraph 10.21 includes awareness of disciplinary action, CCTV, open offices, whistleblowing and restricting personal devices in high-risk areas. Unauthorised disclosure can include photographing screens.

quiz.question: In BNM's 2026 action against Bank Kerjasama Rakyat Malaysia Berhad, which MCIPD failures did BNM's release describe?
options: Weak ICT controls and weak detection of unusual access, viewing or downloads
Failure to answer a police request for customer statements within the time set by the investigating officer
Charging customers fees not disclosed in product terms
Failure to submit cash threshold reports to BNM
quiz.explanation: BNM cited MCIPD paragraphs 10.12, 10.13 and 10.23: preventive and detective ICT controls, their monitoring, and detection of unauthorised access, suspicious viewing or downloads and unauthorised disclosure.

sessions.title: Phishing, Scams and Account Takeover: Protecting Customers and Yourself
sessions.summary: Learn how social engineering targets staff and customers, the RMiT controls that make phishing harder (no links in SMS, device binding, cooling-off, phishing-resistant MFA, fraud detection) and what customer service staff must know under BNM's e-banking fraud policy document.
objectives: Recognise phishing, vishing and other social engineering aimed at bank staff and customers
Explain RMiT's customer-side controls: SMS without links, device binding, cooling-off, MFA and kill switches
Apply Appendix 11 fraud detection duties, including blocking, customer contact and vulnerable customers
Describe what customer service staff must know and tell customers under BNM's e-banking fraud rules

cards.title: Stage three: the scam frontline
cards.setting: Contact centre floor, Cyberjaya. Wednesday, 9:05 am.

lines.text: Line 14 lights up. The caller is crying before the agent finishes the greeting.
Puan Rosnah, 67, from Ipoh. Someone called saying they were from 'the bank's security unit'. They said her account was being used for crime and walked her through 'securing' it on her phone.
RM48,000 left her account in three transfers to accounts she had never heard of. She still thinks she was helping the police.
Classic impersonation scam. The attacker didn't break our systems. They broke her trust, then used our app.
That's why RMiT spends pages on digital fraud. Today you learn the controls, and what Hafiz's team must say in the first five minutes.

scenes.heading: The human door
scenes.narration: Most digital fraud starts with social engineering: a fake message, a convincing call or a cloned website that tricks someone into giving access.

scenes.heading: No links in texts
scenes.narration: RMiT requires banks to remove clickable links from SMS messages to customers, and to tell customers about the change, so any link in a 'bank' text is a warning sign.

scenes.heading: One device, one account
scenes.narration: By default, transactions are authorised from a single bound mobile device. Customers are alerted when a new device or new details appear, and cooling-off periods slow down risky changes.

scenes.heading: Real-time detection
scenes.narration: Fraud analytics must spot and block suspicious transactions in real time, using each customer's risk profile, mule account intelligence and device changes.

scenes.heading: The kill switch
scenes.narration: Customers must have a quick self-service way to freeze their account, and a contact centre resourced to help people in distress.

cards.title: Anatomy of an account takeover, and where controls bite
cards.caption: Each step maps to RMiT controls in paragraph 12 and Appendices 3 and 11.

items.label: Bait
items.detail: Fake SMS, call or ad. Control: no links in bank SMS; customers can verify genuine bank calls.

items.label: Credentials stolen
items.detail: Victim enters details on a fake site. Control: phishing-resistant MFA, more secure than plain SMS codes.

items.label: New device added
items.detail: Fraudster binds his phone. Control: one-device binding, instant alert, cooling-off period.

items.label: Limits raised
items.detail: Fraudster lifts transfer limits. Control: verification and cooling-off for limit increases.

items.label: Money moved to mules
items.detail: Rapid transfers to new payees. Control: real-time detection, blocking and call-back to the customer.

cards.question: A customer receives an SMS that looks like it comes from Bukit Kenanga, with a link to 'update your details'. Why should staff tell customers this is a red flag?
options: RMiT requires banks to remove clickable links from SMS messages to customers
Banks may send links only by email, never by SMS
SMS messages from banks must be in Bahasa Malaysia only
Only BNM may send customers links by SMS
cards.explanation: RMiT requires banks to remove clickable links from SMS to customers and to make customers aware of this, so a link in a 'bank' SMS points to phishing. The other statements are not RMiT rules.

cards.title: Customer-side controls in RMiT Appendix 3
cards.body:
These are the controls your customers meet in the app, and the ones fraudsters try to talk them out of:

- **Device binding**: transactions are authenticated from **one mobile or secure device per account holder** by default, unless an informed customer asks otherwise.
- **Alerts**: customers are told **immediately** when a new device accesses the account or their details change.
- **Cooling-off and verification** for first-time enrolment, new devices, limit increases and abnormal patterns.
- **Conservative default limits** for new customers, with RMiT giving RM1,000 a day as an example, changeable through secure channels.
- **MFA** for financial and high-risk transactions (including adding a favourite payee), using technology **more secure than unencrypted SMS**; codes are generated on the customer's device and tied to the payee and amount.
- **Kill switch**: a secure self-service way to suspend the account (paragraph 12.8).

cards.title: Which control stops which trick?
cards.prompt: Match each fraud trick to the RMiT control designed to stop it.

pairs.left: Fraudster registers his own phone to the victim's account
pairs.right: One-device binding with an instant new-device alert and a cooling-off period

pairs.left: Victim reads out an SMS code to a 'bank officer'
pairs.right: MFA more secure than unencrypted SMS, with codes tied to the payee and amount

pairs.left: Fake bank text with a 'verify now' link
pairs.right: No clickable links in bank SMS, and customer awareness of that rule

pairs.left: Stolen funds sent to a newly opened account
pairs.right: Real-time analytics that flag suspected mule accounts

pairs.left: Customer realises at midnight that the account is compromised
pairs.right: Self-service kill switch to suspend the account

cards.title: Social engineering against staff: red flag or routine?
cards.prompt: The NCII code requires awareness training on social engineering. Sort these requests that reach bank staff.

items.text: 'IT helpdesk' calls and asks you to read out the MFA code just sent to you
An email from the 'CEO' asks you to urgently change a supplier's bank account today
A visitor without a pass asks you to hold the secure door open
A caller claiming to be police demands customer statements by phone
Your manager asks you in person to complete the annual awareness module
The service desk portal shows the ticket you raised has been resolved
A message with a QR code to 'reclaim your staff bonus' on a new website
The bank's internal portal announces the date of the next cyber drill

lines.text: One of my agents, Siti, just got a call. 'IT support' said her account was locked and asked for the code that had just popped up on her phone.
Did she give it?
No! She hung up and called the real service desk number from the intranet. Then she reported it.
Brilliant. The prompt means someone already had her password. We're resetting it and checking where else it was used.
That's the behaviour our training has to build. Now let's see what happens when the customer is the one being manipulated.

cards.title: The blocked transfer
cards.situation: At 3:12 pm Bukit Kenanga's fraud engine blocks a RM30,000 transfer from Encik Lim, 72, to a payee added 20 minutes earlier from a new device. Encik Lim then calls Hafiz's team insisting the transfer is genuine and urgent: 'an investment officer' is on his other phone line. What should the agent do?

choices.text: Keep the hold, ask open questions to check whether a third party is directing him, explain current scam patterns, and escalate to the fraud team before any release
choices.outcome: Best response. Appendix 11 requires verification before releasing flagged transactions, including checks for customers acting under a fraudster's influence, and higher risk scoring for vulnerable customers.

choices.text: Release the transfer, because the customer has confirmed it is genuine
choices.outcome: A confirmation given while a fraudster is on the other line is not real consent. Releasing it ignores RMiT's requirement to detect coercion during verification.

choices.text: Keep the hold but end the call quickly, telling him to visit a branch next week
choices.outcome: The hold protects the money, but the customer is left confused and the scam may continue. RMiT expects touch points to give prompt advice and connect him to the fraud team.

choices.text: Close his account immediately without explaining why
choices.outcome: Disproportionate and unhelpful. He needs guidance and a way to restore access after robust verification, as Appendix 11 requires.

cards.title: Numbers from RMiT's fraud rules
cards.caption: From RMiT Appendices 3 and 11 and the footnote to paragraph 12.5.

items.label: Clickable links in bank SMS
items.detail: Banks must remove them and tell customers about the change.

items.label: Bound device per account holder
items.detail: Default for authorising digital transactions, unless an informed customer opts out.

items.label: To contact the customer
items.detail: After a suspicious transaction is blocked, even at peak times.

items.label: Fraud playbook update
items.detail: Updated and validated at least once a year, using lessons from missed frauds.

cards.title: Safety messages customers must keep hearing

cards.back: Read transaction alerts promptly, check balances and statements regularly, and report anything unauthorised at once.
Treat unexpected messages as suspect: do not click, do not share codes, do not pay and do not download from unknown sources.

cards.front: Is this call really the bank?
cards.back: Banks must give customers practical ways to verify that a call from the bank or its agents is genuine.
Banks must give customers a hotline or similar service to report e-banking fraud, shown clearly on the website and app.
Use the self-service kill switch to suspend the account, then call the bank to restore access after verification.

cards.question: Under BNM's policy document on fair treatment for victims of unauthorised e-banking transactions, what must banks ensure about customer service staff?
options: They are well aware of current fraud risks and the bank's end-to-end fraud investigation process
They decide whether the bank refunds the customer on the call
They refer every fraud victim to the police before taking any action
They are certified fraud examiners
cards.explanation: Paragraph 8.3 requires customer service personnel to be well aware of current fraud risks and the investigation process so they can advise customers on frauds, scams and identity theft. It does not make them the refund decision-makers.

cards.title: The first five minutes with a scam victim
cards.body:
When a customer calls about a possible scam:

1. **Stop the bleeding**: help them use the kill switch or suspend access now.
2. **Stay calm and kind**: victims feel ashamed. Do not blame.
3. **Check for a live scammer**: ask if anyone else is on the line or guiding them.
4. **Capture facts**: times, amounts, payees, devices, messages received.
5. **Escalate** to the fraud team through the playbook, and explain what happens next.
6. **Never** ask for full passwords or codes, even to 'verify'.

cards.title: Stage three take-aways
items: Social engineering is the main route into accounts; NCII entities must train staff on it, and every bank's awareness programme should cover it.
RMiT requires no clickable links in bank SMS, one-device binding by default, instant alerts and cooling-off for risky changes.
MFA for transactions must be more secure than unencrypted SMS, with codes tied to the payee and amount.
Fraud engines must block suspicious transactions in real time; banks notify the customer at once and aim to reach them within 30 minutes.
Customer service staff must know current fraud risks and the investigation process so they can guide victims.

cards.prompt: Think of a suspicious message or call you received at work or at home. What made it convincing? How would you explain the warning signs to an older relative or a new colleague?

quiz.question: What does RMiT require banks to do about hyperlinks in SMS messages to customers?
options: Shorten them so customers can read them more easily
Add a warning line underneath each link
Remove clickable hyperlinks and make customers aware of the change
Send them only during office hours
quiz.explanation: The footnote to paragraph 12.5 requires banks to remove clickable hyperlinks from SMS messages to customers and to create awareness of this change, reducing phishing risk.

quiz.question: By default, how many devices may be used to authenticate a retail customer's digital transactions under RMiT Appendix 3?
options: Up to three devices, as long as all of them are registered on the same day at a branch
Any device on which the customer can log in with a password
One mobile or secure device per account holder, unless the customer opts out
Two devices: one phone and one computer
quiz.explanation: Appendix 3 requires secure binding that restricts transaction authentication by default to one mobile or secure device per account holder, with exceptions only for customers who understand and accept the risks.

quiz.question: What must happen when a customer's account is accessed from a new device or their contact details are changed?
options: The customer must be alerted immediately
The bank must close the account for 30 days
The bank must report it to BNM within two hours
Nothing, unless a transaction above RM10,000 follows
quiz.explanation: Appendix 3 requires all customers to be alerted immediately when access from a new device is detected or their details are changed. A BNM notification relates to cyber incidents, not routine device changes.

quiz.question: Which statement about MFA for financial transactions matches RMiT Appendix 3?
options: SMS one-time passwords are the preferred method for all transactions
MFA technology and channels must be more secure than unencrypted SMS
MFA is required only for transfers above RM50,000
MFA codes should be generated by the bank's server and sent to the customer
quiz.explanation: Appendix 3 requires MFA that resists phishing, deployed through channels more secure than unencrypted SMS, and OTPs generated on the customer's device and bound to the transaction details, not on the bank's server.

quiz.question: A fraud engine blocks a suspicious transfer. What does RMiT Appendix 11 require regarding the customer?
options: Wait for the customer to notice the blocked transfer and call the bank's hotline to ask about it
Contact the customer within three working days by letter
Notify the customer at once and aim to reach them within 30 minutes
Release the transfer after 24 hours if the customer does not respond
quiz.explanation: Appendix 11 requires immediate notification of each block and enough resources to contact the affected customer within 30 minutes of the transaction, including at peak times, with a process for when the customer cannot be reached.

quiz.question: During a call-back on a flagged transfer, the customer seems to be repeating words someone else is telling him. What does RMiT expect the verification procedure to include?
options: Immediate release of the transfer, because the customer has passed authentication on the app
Transfer of the call to the police before speaking further
A requirement that the customer visit a branch with two witnesses
Ways to detect that a fraudster may be influencing the customer
quiz.explanation: Appendix 11 says verification procedures must include ways to detect circumstances where a customer may be responding under the influence or threat of fraudsters.

quiz.question: How does RMiT Appendix 11 treat vulnerable customers such as senior citizens or previous fraud victims in fraud analytics?
options: They must be excluded from digital banking
They must use branch services only for transfers
A higher risk score must be applied to them
Their transactions must always be approved by a relative
quiz.explanation: Appendix 11 requires higher risk scoring for vulnerable customers, for example senior citizens, younger customers, previous fraud victims and those with lower awareness of e-banking safety.

quiz.question: What must customer service personnel be aware of under paragraph 8.3 of BNM's policy document on victims of unauthorised e-banking transactions?
options: The personal details of every fraud investigator in the bank
The bank's capital adequacy ratio and liquidity position
The source code of the mobile banking application
Current fraud risks and the bank's end-to-end fraud investigation process
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 8.3 requires customer service staff to be well aware of current fraud risks and the end-to-end investigation process so they can advise customers on frauds, scams and identity theft.

quiz.question: A colleague receives an MFA prompt on her phone that she did not request, followed by a call from 'IT' asking for the code. What is the best response?
options: Give the code, since IT staff need it to unlock accounts quickly during an outage
Refuse, hang up, report it and change the password
Approve the prompt so that the notifications stop
Ignore both and carry on working
quiz.explanation: An unrequested MFA prompt usually means the password is already compromised. Sharing or approving it hands over the account; reporting lets the security team reset credentials and investigate.

quiz.question: How often must a bank's fraud management playbook be updated and validated under RMiT Appendix 11?
options: Once every three years with the IT policies
At least once a year, or more often if needed
Only when BNM issues a new circular
Every five years as part of the strategic plan
quiz.explanation: Appendix 11 requires a comprehensive fraud management playbook updated and validated at least once a year, reflecting confirmed fraud cases and frauds the bank failed to detect.

sessions.title: When It Goes Wrong: Cyber Incidents, Customer Information Breaches and Notification Clocks
sessions.summary: Respond to a live incident: RMiT's incident response plan, CERT and cyber drills, notifying BNM within two hours of confirming a cyber incident, the NACSA clock for NCII entities, MCIPD's breach rules and the PDPA duty to notify the Commissioner and affected customers.
objectives: Describe RMiT's cyber incident response plan, the CERT, out-of-band communication and the annual cyber drill
Apply the notification clocks: BNM for cyber incidents, NACSA for NCII entities, and BNM under MCIPD
Decide when a customer information breach must be notified to BNM immediately and what the notice contains
Apply the amended PDPA's breach notification duty and MCIPD's rules on investigation and customer notices

cards.title: Stage four: the crisis room
cards.setting: Crisis room, Bukit Kenanga head office. Thursday, 7:50 am.

lines.text: Remember the 2 am downloads from stage two? This morning a screenshot is circulating on social media: a spreadsheet of Bukit Kenanga customers with names, IC numbers and loan balances.
It matches the files pulled with LN4471's credentials. Phishing stole his password two weeks ago. About 1,800 customers are in the sample.
That's a customer information breach of significant scale, and it's public. Under MCIPD we notify BNM immediately. Under the PDPA I notify the Commissioner as soon as practicable.
And it started with an intrusion using stolen credentials. If we confirm it's a cyber incident, the two-hour clock to BNM starts at confirmation.
(joining by phone) I want the board told today. What do we know, what don't we know, and who are we calling?
Let's walk the playbook, step by step. Every minute counts now.

cards.title: Who must hear about it, and when

scenes.heading: BNM: cyber incidents
scenes.narration: RMiT points to BNM's business continuity rules: all cyber incidents must be notified to BNM within two hours of confirming the incident, through BNM's central email channel and its cyber incident scoring form.

scenes.heading: BNM: customer information
scenes.narration: Under MCIPD, a customer information breach that threatens reputation or public confidence, may cause significant harm, or affects more than a thousand customers must be notified to BNM immediately.

scenes.heading: NACSA: if you are NCII
scenes.narration: A bank designated as national critical information infrastructure must also alert NACSA immediately, submit details within six hours through the NC4 portal, and add supplementary information within fourteen days.

scenes.heading: The PDP Commissioner
scenes.narration: Under the amended PDPA, a data controller that has reason to believe a personal data breach has happened must notify the Commissioner as soon as practicable.

scenes.heading: The customers
scenes.narration: Where significant harm is likely, affected customers must be told without undue delay, in plain language, with steps they can take to protect themselves.

cards.title: The notification clocks
cards.caption: Based on BNM's BCM and MCIPD policy documents, RMiT Appendix 12 and PDPA section 12B. Your bank's playbook sets internal deadlines inside these.

items.label: BNM under MCIPD
items.detail: Breach that is significant in reputation, harm or scale; give what is known, with estimates.

items.label: NACSA alert (NCII only)
items.detail: Authorised persons report that an incident has or may have occurred.

items.label: BNM cyber incident notice
items.detail: From confirming the incident, by email with the scoring form; update as facts emerge.

items.label: NC4 portal details (NCII)
items.detail: Required information on the incident submitted through the NC4 portal.

items.label: PDP Commissioner
items.detail: As soon as practicable once there is reason to believe a breach occurred.

items.label: NACSA supplementary (NCII)
items.detail: Further information, as complete as practicable, after the notification.

cards.question: Under BNM's Business Continuity Management policy document, which RMiT cross-refers to, when must a bank notify BNM of a cyber incident?
options: Within 2 hours upon confirmation of the incident
Within 24 hours of the first alert
Within 72 hours after the investigation is complete
Only if more than 1,000 customers are affected
cards.explanation: Paragraph 10.5 of the BCM policy document requires all cyber incidents to be notified within 2 hours upon confirmation, after a preliminary check that the incident is cyber-related. The 1,000-customer threshold belongs to MCIPD's breach rules.

cards.title: RMiT's incident response machinery
cards.body:
RMiT (paragraphs 11.12 to 11.16) requires a bank to be ready **before** the crisis:

- **Cyber crisis management** built into the bank's crisis plan, escalation, business continuity and disaster recovery, with a **communication plan** for shareholders, regulators, customers and employees.
- A **Cyber Incident Response Plan** covering preparedness, detection and analysis (including preserving forensic evidence and testing a threat actor's claims), containment and eradication, recovery, and post-incident review.
- A **CERT** whose members know the plan and are **contactable at all times**.
- **Out-of-band communication** that still works if email and phones are compromised.
- An **annual cyber drill** with the board, senior management and relevant third parties, testing escalation, communication and decisions, with results reported to the board.

For affected customers, paragraph 12.9 adds closer monitoring of their accounts, notifying them, and reissuing compromised credentials or cards.

cards.title: Which MCIPD trigger for immediate notice to BNM?
cards.prompt: Each breach below must be notified to BNM immediately under MCIPD paragraph 11.8. Sort it by the main trigger it meets.

items.text: Customer list screenshots are circulating on social media
A well-known public figure's account details are leaked
Customer data is disclosed to a party suspected of crime
Online banking login credentials of customers are exposed
Customers' fingerprint templates are stolen from a vendor
Data that could enable identity theft is lost
Letters to 3,200 customers are posted to the wrong addresses
A file of 1,500 customers is emailed to the wrong vendor

lines.text: Could we wait until Monday to tell BNM? By then we'll know the exact number of customers and the full root cause.
MCIPD says immediately. If we don't have everything, we send what we have now, including an estimate of how many customers are affected, and then the rest as soon as we get it.
Same for the cyber notice: two hours from confirmation, then progressive updates. BNM would rather have a rough picture early than a perfect one late.
And my agents need a script before customers start calling. MCIPD says staff must be trained to handle their questions.

cards.title: Friday evening: what goes to BNM?
cards.situation: It is Friday, 6 pm. Bukit Kenanga has confirmed that about 1,800 customers' identity and loan data were stolen using a phished credential and posted online. Forensics will take weeks. The final customer count is uncertain. The communications team suggests waiting for the full picture before contacting regulators.

choices.text: Notify BNM now with what is known, including an estimated customer count; notify the PDP Commissioner as soon as practicable; prepare customer notices and an agent script
choices.outcome: Correct. MCIPD paragraph 11.17 expects immediate notice with available information and an estimate, followed by the complete details without undue delay. PDPA section 12B runs alongside.

choices.text: Notify BNM on Monday with a complete and verified report
choices.outcome: Too late. A breach of significant scale that is public must be notified immediately; completeness is not a reason to delay.

choices.text: Notify BNM now but leave the PDP Commissioner until the investigation report is ready
choices.outcome: BNM is covered, but MCIPD reminds banks that, as data controllers, they must also meet the PDPA's notification duty, which is as soon as practicable.

choices.text: Tell affected customers first, then decide whether regulators need to know
choices.outcome: MCIPD expects customer notification without undue delay after the BNM notice, not instead of it.

cards.title: BNM under MCIPD versus the PDP Commissioner under the PDPA
cards.caption: Both duties can apply to the same incident. MCIPD's footnote expressly reminds banks of PDPA section 12B.

items.label: When
items.left: Immediately, if the breach meets a reputation, harm or scale trigger
items.right: As soon as practicable once there is reason to believe a breach occurred

items.label: Customers
items.left: Notify without undue delay after BNM, where significant harm is likely
items.right: Notify data subjects without unnecessary delay where significant harm is likely

items.label: Follow-up
items.left: Root-cause investigation within 3 months; report to board, then BNM
items.right: In the manner and form the Commissioner determines

items.label: Sanction
items.left: Enforcement under the FSA for breaching standards
items.right: Failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence: fine up to RM250,000, prison up to 2 years, or both

cards.title: Handling a customer information breach under MCIPD
cards.prompt: Put the bank's steps in a sensible order.
steps: Staff spot the breach (or a complaint reveals it) and escalate at once
Assess impact: intent, data type, number of customers, recipients, misuse risk
Notify BNM immediately if a trigger is met, with estimates where needed
Notify affected customers without undue delay where significant harm is likely
Investigate the root cause within three months and table the report to the board
Record the breach and lessons in the breach register

cards.back: What happened and the data affected; number of customers; actual and potential harm; measures taken or planned.
Brief description; possible consequences; steps the customer should take; what the bank is doing; contact details for help.
Directly, for example by email or app notification. Public notices only where direct contact is disproportionate, or until affected customers are identified.
If the breach appears to involve fraud, crime or identity theft, notify the relevant agency as soon as practicable.
If the breach involves data from another financial service provider, promptly notify that provider.
Record every breach with root causes, remedial actions and lessons; keep investigation reports at least seven years.

cards.question: Under MCIPD, how long does a bank have to complete its investigation into a customer information breach, and when is the report sent to BNM for a breach of significant scale?
options: Three months to complete; sent to BNM within one working day after it is tabled to the board
Fourteen days to complete; sent to BNM within one month
Six months to complete; sent to BNM only if BNM asks for it
One month to complete; sent to BNM before the board sees it
cards.explanation: Paragraphs 11.19 and 11.20 require the investigation to be completed within three months of detection and tabled to the board, with the report sent to BNM within one working day of tabling where the breach causes significant harm, exceeds 1,000 customers, or involves deliberate disclosure.

cards.title: Example: Bukit Kenanga's customer notice
cards.body:
This is the quest's own fictional notice, written to meet MCIPD paragraphs 11.27 and 11.28:

> **We are writing to tell you about a security incident affecting your information.** On 9 October, we found that an unauthorised person used a staff member's stolen password to copy files containing your name, identity card number and loan balance. Your online banking password was **not** included.
>
> **What this could mean**: criminals may contact you pretending to be the bank.
>
> **What you should do**: never share codes or passwords; check your alerts and statements; be wary of calls and messages about your loan.
>
> **What we are doing**: we have closed the access, increased monitoring of your account and reported the incident to the authorities.
>
> **Questions?** Call our dedicated line shown in the app.

Plain language, no blame-shifting, and practical steps first.

cards.title: Stage four take-aways
items: Cyber incidents go to BNM within 2 hours of confirmation through the central channel and scoring form, with progressive updates.
NCII entities also alert NACSA immediately, submit details within 6 hours via the NC4 portal and add supplementary information within 14 days.
MCIPD: notify BNM immediately if a breach threatens reputation or confidence, may cause significant harm, or affects over 1,000 customers; send estimates if needed.
PDPA s.12B: notify the PDP Commissioner as soon as practicable, and data subjects without unnecessary delay where significant harm is likely.
Investigate within three months, table to the board, send qualifying reports to BNM within one working day, and keep a breach register.

cards.prompt: If you discovered a possible breach at 5 pm on a Friday, do you know exactly who to call and how? Write down your bank's escalation route, and check it against your playbook this week.

quiz.question: RMiT paragraph 11.18 requires cyber incidents to be notified to BNM in line with which documents?
options: The Personal Data Protection Act only, because every cyber incident involves personal data
The Cyber Security Act 2024 only
The bank's own incident policy, with no BNM template
BNM's Operational Risk Reporting and BCM policy documents, among others
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.18 points to Operational Risk Reporting Part C, Business Continuity Management Part C and other relevant BNM documents. The PDPA and the Cyber Security Act impose separate duties.

quiz.question: Through which channel must a bank notify BNM of cyber and non-cyber incidents under the BCM policy document?
options: BNM's centralised incident email, with the required form
A letter to the Governor's office by courier, followed by a meeting with the supervisors
A post on the bank's corporate website
A call to the BNM contact centre hotline only
quiz.explanation: The BCM document requires notification through the centralised email, with the Cyber Incident Scoring System form for cyber incidents. Calls to relationship managers are an accepted fallback only when email is unavailable.

quiz.question: What must the CERT members be, under RMiT paragraph 11.14?
options: External consultants appointed by BNM to lead every response
Familiar with the response plan and reachable at all times
Members of the board audit committee
Available only during office hours
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.14 requires relevant CERT members to know the incident response plan and handling procedures and to remain contactable at all times.

quiz.question: Who must be involved in the annual cyber drill under RMiT paragraph 11.16?
options: Only the security operations centre team, since drills are a technical exercise for responders
Only BNM's examiners and the external auditor
Only customers who volunteer to test the app
The board, senior management and relevant third-party providers
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.16 requires an annual drill testing the incident response plan and out-of-band communication, involving the board, senior management and relevant third parties, with results reported to the board.

quiz.question: Under MCIPD, above how many affected customers is a customer information breach considered of significant scale?
options: More than 100 customers
More than 1,000 customers
More than 10,000 customers
More than 500 customers
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.11 treats a breach as significant scale when affected customers exceed one thousand.

quiz.question: A bank confirms a breach of 1,400 customers' data but does not yet know the exact number. What does MCIPD require?
options: Wait until the exact number is confirmed by forensics, then notify BNM with the full verified picture
Notify BNM now with what is known and an estimate, then complete it promptly
Notify only the PDP Commissioner, since BNM needs exact numbers
Notify BNM within three months with the investigation report
quiz.explanation: Paragraph 11.17 says incomplete information is no reason to wait: the bank provides what it has immediately, an estimated count, and the rest as soon as it is obtained.

quiz.question: Which of these does MCIPD give as an example of sensitive customer information whose breach is treated as likely to cause significant harm?
options: The branch where the customer opened the account
The customer's preferred language for statements
The date the customer last visited a branch
Security credentials used to access a customer's account
quiz.explanation: MCIPD gives security credentials, biometric data and medical or health information as examples of sensitive customer information. A breach involving such data is treated as likely to cause significant harm.

quiz.question: When must a data controller notify the Personal Data Protection Commissioner of a personal data breach under the amended PDPA?
options: As soon as practicable once it has reason to believe a breach occurred
Within 30 days after its internal investigation into the breach is complete and signed off
Only when more than 1,000 data subjects are affected
Only after the affected data subjects have been told
quiz.explanation: Section 12B(1) requires notice as soon as practicable once the controller has reason to believe a personal data breach has occurred. The 1,000 threshold is MCIPD's significant scale test for BNM.

quiz.question: An NCII-designated bank detects a serious cyber security incident. Under RMiT Appendix 12, within what time must its authorised persons submit the required information through the NC4 portal?
options: Within two working days of the incident
Within 14 days of the incident
Within one month of the incident
Within six hours of the incident coming to the bank's knowledge
quiz.explanation: Appendix 12 requires an immediate alert, the required information through the NC4 portal within six hours of knowledge, and supplementary information within 14 days of the notification.

quiz.question: Under MCIPD, how must affected customers normally be notified of a breach likely to cause them significant harm?
options: Directly, such as by email or app, without undue delay after the BNM notice
Only through a notice in a national newspaper and on the bank's website, whatever the number affected
Only if the customer asks the bank whether they were affected
Only after the three-month investigation is complete
quiz.explanation: Paragraphs 11.25 and 11.29 require direct notification without undue delay after the BNM notice. Public announcements are for exceptional cases where direct notice is disproportionate or customers are not yet identified.

sessions.title: Third Parties, Cloud, the Amended PDPA and Readiness for BNM
sessions.summary: Close the quest by managing technology risk beyond the bank's walls (third-party providers, outsourcing approvals and cloud), applying the amended PDPA's principles, data protection officer and transfer rules, and assembling the evidence BNM expects from the bank's programme.
objectives: Explain RMiT and outsourcing duties for third-party providers, including service agreement terms and BNM approval
Describe RMiT's cloud risk assessment and the duty to consult BNM before first adopting public cloud for critical systems
Apply the amended PDPA: the seven principles, data processors, data protection officers and transfers abroad
Summarise the reviews, audits, records and training evidence that show BNM the programme works

cards.title: Stage five: the supervisors' gate
cards.setting: Board technology committee, Bukit Kenanga head office. Monday, 3:00 pm.

lines.text: One month to go before BNM's supervisors arrive. The committee agenda has two items: a cloud proposal, and 'Are we ready?'
Management wants to move the loan origination system, a critical system, to a public cloud provider. It would be our first critical system on public cloud.
Then RMiT says we consult BNM first, after a full risk assessment, a readiness confirmation and an independent pre-implementation review.
And customer data will sit with the provider, so MCIPD's outsourced provider rules and the PDPA apply. The provider is our data processor.
I also need their incident data in real time. If they get hit, I can't wait for a monthly report.
Good. Let's get this right, then prove to BNM that everything we've learned actually runs.

cards.title: Your risk does not leave with your data

scenes.heading: Still accountable
